1771601: The Captain and I made a go around on our second attempt to landing. The first approach was discontinued due to RVR being reported below the minimums for the approach outside the final approach fix. Due to a glideslope anomaly on Runway 23. The glideslope a few hundred feet from reaching minimums made a quick movement towards half scale deflection down. The aircraft was on a constant rate of descent, airspeed and proper configuration, hand flown below 1700 feet per approach plate. At the point that I called runway in sight the Captain and I noticed that the aircraft was not going to touch down in the prescribed TDZ and accomplished the go around procedure. While being vectored for a 3rd attempt at landing, the Captain and I briefed that if the anomaly happened again, we would accomplished another go around. Before the 3rd approach, another flight was able to land on their first attempt. After requesting a PIREP from the crew, they said they were able to see the runway right at minimums. We were able to obtain visual reference with the runway right at minimums and complete a successful landing. In the hotel van with the other crew we asked them if they had issues with the glideslope and mentioned they did. They said it acted very similarly to our situation. It seems that this has been a recurring theme at CRW in the past as well. The cause of the second go-around was due to an inaccurate indication of the glideslope that put the crew in a situation where a landing would have been made outside of the TDZ. I think the FAA needs to take a deeper dive in what is causing glideslope anomalies for the ILS 23 into CRW. Especially coming into the winter months in mountainous areas where weather can deteriorate rapidly.
1771628: We were cleared for the visual approach Runway 17 into Asheville. We were at 6000 feet coming in from the southeast and we had the GPS runway 17 loaded in the FMS. The Captain set 4000 ft in the Altitude Selector and we looked at the GPS plate confirmed 4000 ft at FAF and saw the highest obstacle of 4368 ft to our right in the distance. We were VMC at night and we saw the higher terrain to the right of us and we saw [lower] terrain in front of us. We both thought we could get through with the [lower] terrain ahead. As we crossed over the [lower] terrain we got the GPWS 'terrain' and pull up. The Captain quickly clicked off the autopilot and arrested the descent at 4700 ft MSL. No limitations were exceeded as we were at Flap 8. We continued on the approach and landed without further incident. We saw the higher terrain to our left which I pointed out and we both agreed we could set the FAF altitude and descend. The Captain even slowed his descent to 0.9 from 1.5 as we crossed the terrain. We may have been too focused on the highest obstacle and higher terrain. We clicked off the autopilot and I called out the altitude we were at cleared his FD. We continued since we arrested the descent and no further incident took place. Next time I will suggest to wait until we cross over the terrain before descending from 6000 feet.
1771639: We briefed the route and departure, to include the [engine failure] procedures. We confirmed the route in the FMS. After being cleared for takeoff and reaching 400 AGL, We turned to heading 189 and hit moderate or greater turbulence and mountain waves, which significantly affected us. I had trouble communicating with ATC and performing cockpit duties due to turbulence. Just before reaching 1,000 AGL, Tower said switch to departure. Upon contacting departure we were told 'upon reaching 8,000, proceed direct to a fix', but the radio quality of the transmission was poor and we couldn't clearly hear the name of the fix. I realized the mountain was on our path and for an immediate left turn to avoid terrain. The Spokane Departure Controller cleared us direct to a fix by name but not the identifier or phonetic spelling, which I couldn't understand due to significant turbulence and poor radio quality. We continued normal flap retraction callouts and takeoff profile. We were given heading a 120, to which we turned, and it took several radio calls between the Captain and ATC to get clarification on the identifier to which we were cleared. This was due to scratchy radios, the turbulence, and some possible confusion on the part of the controller who was talking with us and another company aircraft. We were mistakenly trying to navigate to ENY VOR which caused us to be confused and task saturated. Once we got the correct identifier for HIA and entered into the FMS, we proceeded on course as cleared. However this delay resulted in us temporarily deviating from the charted procedure. This caused the controller to get a low altitude alert although we did not receive any terrain avoidance warnings from our aircraft. In retrospect, the controller admitted on our phone conversation afterwards that this situation is very common. There are a lot of risks and stressors associated with this MZULA.MSO RWY12 and I feel like our outside resources did not help the flight crew. We accept full responsibility for allowing this situation to develop, but changes to this procedure will greatly increase safety in the future.First our Jeppesen charts had no verbal narrative and left us needing FAA charts to understand the procedure. It would be a great help if the procedure could be simplified or the controller's expectations that are outside the procedure could be communicated before we hit significant turbulence. The controller was clearly frustrated with us which only made our situation worse by trying to give us a phone number during a high stress and high workload phase of flight in significant turbulence. This shows the controllers are not fully aware of what human factors the flight crews have and how to help safety of flight. Having poor radio transmission quality was also a significant factor. I was the First Officer and Pilot Flying departing MSO. I received and read back the clearance from ATC which included the MZULA5 Departure MSO transition. I programmed this into our FMS and the Captain and I thoroughly reviewed the route in the FMS and on our Jeppesen plates. We also briefed the procedure for engine failure departure. In my takeoff briefing I again described the departure we were assigned. After being cleared for takeoff and reaching 400 AGL, I turned to heading 189 as charted. Immediately we began to encounter moderate turbulence. Just before reaching 1,000 ft AGL, Tower said switch to Departure. Upon contacting Departure we were told 'upon reaching 8,000, proceed direct to ________ ' but it was very turbulent and we did not clearly hear the name of the fix. I immediately realized the flight director was not commanding a left turn in accordance with the charted procedure. The Captain asked to say again the fix, and the controller said the name but not the identifier or phonetic spelling. At 1,000 ft AGL, I called out 'flight level change', followed by the normal flap retraction callouts and told him we needed a left turn since I knew from the charted SID that's what we were supposed to do. Meanwhile the Captain was trying to get clarification on the fix to which we were to proceed. We knew it would be a left turn so he asked for a left turn and we were given heading 120, to which we turned. During this entire time it was very turbulent and took a lot of effort and concentration to focus on safe flying. It took several radio calls between the Captain and ATC to get clarification on the identifier to which we were cleared. This was due to scratchy radios, the turbulence, and some possible confusion on the part of the controller who was talking with us and another company aircraft. 1771726: After a diversion to our planned alternate we had a routine enroute and descent phase. We contacted Tower on about a 10 mile final. Very shortly after that, at 1050 ft. we received a 'DESCEND DESCEND' TCAS Resolution Alert. The First Officer followed the TCAS guidance and I informed ATC. We were one dot low on the glide slope but correcting and all other approach criteria were stable so I quickly asked the First Officer if he felt stable. He responded that he did, so we agreed that we were okay to continue the approach. At our closest point, the helicopter was directly above us and approximately 200 ft. above, leading to a significantly reduced margin of separation.This event was caused by several factors. The helicopter pilot had us in sight and was maintaining visual separation, but in our opinion, the separation provided was not adequate. I was not able to visually identify the traffic until the Traffic Alert occurred, and at that point there was very little we could do to avoid a loss of separation. I do not believe we should have been sequenced by air traffic control to pass directly underneath the medevac's flight path. After landing I communicated my concerns to tower and he said that once the helicopter reported maintaining Visual Separation, he had no further responsibility to separate us. If that is correct, I believe it is a fundamentally unsafe procedure. In this event it led to us receiving a descending RA at 1000 ft. leaving us with very little maneuvering room. I should have made more of an effort to find the traffic prior to receiving a Traffic Alert, but with the city lights it was difficult. This was at the end of a very high workload, 3 hour blocked flight with significant weather, holding, a diversion, and fuel considerations. I believe that this type of event could have been prevented with better planning from air traffic control. There was clearly a difference in expectations between the helicopter pilot and us, and the helicopter pilot may have been comfortable with 200 ft. of separation, but we were not. We diverted due to weather. On final approach we received a TCAS Resolution Alert due to a medical helicopter crossing the final approach. I was Pilot Flying for the approach. When we received the Traffic Alert, I initially assumed it was an aircraft on a parallel approach. The Pilot Monitoring reported the aircraft in sight. The helicopter had also reported us in sight. The helicopter passed approximately 200 ft. above. I don't recall ever hearing a clear of conflict call. I was manually flying a challenging approach due to high winds and did not recognize the threat until a few seconds before the Resolution Alert.
